title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, what you do and which languages you speak — and spot the single pattern behind every Danish verb in the present tense.
bekal: say where you're from (*jeg kommer fra*) and where you live (*jeg bor i*)
state your job without an article: *jeg er lærer*
form the present tense of any verb yourself: base form + **-r**

dialogs.title: Dialogue — I kantinen
dialogs.intro: Lunch break in the school cafeteria. Mette and Budi sit with Ahmad, another student.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Budi, det her er Ahmad. Han går også på sprogskolen.
lines.id: Budi, this is Ahmad. He's at the language school too.
lines.literal: Budi, this here is Ahmad. he goes also on language-school-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hej Ahmad! Hvor kommer du fra?
lines.id: Hi Ahmad! Where are you from?
lines.literal: hi Ahmad! where come you from?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jeg kommer fra Syrien, men jeg bor i Aarhus nu.
lines.id: I'm from Syria, but I live in Aarhus now.
lines.literal: I come from Syria, but I live in Aarhus now.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvor længe har du boet i Danmark?
lines.id: How long have you lived in Denmark?
lines.literal: how long have you lived in Denmark?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: I to år. Og du? Hvad laver du her?
lines.id: For two years. And you? What do you do here?
lines.literal: in two years. and you? what make you here?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg studerer i København. Jeg læser arkitektur.
lines.id: I'm a student in Copenhagen. I'm studying architecture.
lines.literal: I study in Copenhagen. I read architecture.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.id: Interesting. Do you speak English too?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, jeg taler engelsk og indonesisk. Og lidt dansk!
lines.id: Yes, I speak English and Indonesian. And a little Danish!
lines.literal: yes, I speak English and Indonesian. and little Danish!

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Du taler faktisk rigtig godt dansk.
lines.id: Your Danish is actually really good.
lines.literal: you speak actually really well Danish.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tak! Men jeg forstår ikke altid, når I taler hurtigt.
lines.id: Thanks! But I don't always understand when you talk fast.
lines.literal: thanks! but I understand not always, when you(pl) speak fast.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Det gør jeg heller ikke. Vi lærer sammen.
lines.id: Neither do I. We're learning together.
lines.literal: that do I either not. we learn together.

notes: **Kommer fra or er fra?** Both are correct. *Jeg er fra Indonesien* states your origin as a fact; *jeg kommer fra Indonesien* is a little livelier, like "I come from". In everyday speech they're interchangeable.

**Bor, not lever.** *At bo* = to live somewhere, to have an address there. *At leve* = to be alive. "I live in Aarhus" is always *jeg bor i Aarhus*; *jeg lever i Aarhus* sounds as if you're barely surviving there.

**Jobs without an article.** *Jeg er lærer*, not *jeg er en lærer*. This is the opposite of English (*I am a teacher*) — and a classic mistake for English speakers. The article only appears when there's a description: *jeg er **en** god lærer*.

**Læser arkitektur.** *At læse* does mean "to read", but with a field of study it means "to study, to major in" — like British "to read law". *Jeg læser medicin* = I'm studying medicine. Unexpected, and very common.
**Faktisk** isn't "in fact" so much as "actually" — used for something slightly unexpected, exactly like English *actually*. Danes use it constantly.

**Heller ikke** = "not … either", "neither". Danish doesn't say *også ikke*; there's a separate word for "too" in a negative sentence, just like English *either*. Compare: *jeg taler også dansk* (I speak Danish too) and *jeg taler heller ikke dansk* (I don't speak Danish either).

**Det gør jeg heller ikke** — look at the order. The sentence starts with *det*, so the subject (*jeg*) jumps behind the verb. This is the most important rule in Danish, and all of Unit 10 is devoted to it. For now just notice that it sounds natural — a bit like English "so do I".
**Når**, not *hvornår*. *Hvornår* asks about time ("when?"), *når* links clauses ("when, whenever"). Two words that are easy to mix up.

grammars.title: Present tense: base form + -r
body: This is the biggest time-saver in all of Danish verb grammar. Take the base form, add **-r**, done — and the result works for every person at once.
after: *Jeg bor, du bor, han bor, vi bor, I bor, de bor* — one form, six persons. Compare English, which still has *he lives*, or Spanish with six different forms.
A base form that already ends in *-r* sometimes takes nothing more: *at høre* → *hører*, but *at gøre* → *gør* (not *gører*).

⚠️ Only a handful of verbs don't follow this pattern, and they're all among the most common: *at være* → **er**, *at have* → **har**, *at vide* → **ved**, *at gøre* → **gør**, plus the four modal verbs *kan*, *skal*, *vil*, *må* covered in Unit 13.

grammars.title: Saying where you're from, where you live, what you do
body: Three sentence frames you'll repeat hundreds of times:
after: **i** for countries and cities: *i Danmark*, *i Jakarta*. **på** for islands: *på Fyn*, *på Bali*, *på Java*. The island rule can be surprising, but it's handy — Denmark itself is largely made of islands.
One exception simply has to be memorized as it is: **på Sjælland** (the island Copenhagen is on), but **i København**.

blocks.text: Notice that the three columns have different forms. The country is capitalized; the other two columns are lowercase.
Language names are used **without an article** after *at tale*: *jeg taler dansk*. To say "in Danish", use *på dansk*: *Hvad hedder det på dansk?*

blocks.title: Why these names matter sooner than you think
items: At a Danish language school, the first question you'll hear from other students is almost always *Hvor kommer du fra?* — and the second, *Hvor længe har du været her?*
If you have answers ready for both, your first day becomes much easier.

blocks.text: Some jobs have a separate female form (*en sygeplejerske*), but modern Danish tends to drop the difference. *En lærer* is used for men and women alike, and that's the safe form.

items: De kommer fra en by ____ Java.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: Hvor kommer du fra? — Jeg kommer fra Indonesien. — Jeg bor i København nu. — Jeg er lærer. — Taler du dansk? — Jeg forstår ikke altid.
